title: Reading a Q–Q plot
dek: Sample order statistics against theoretical quantiles of a named reference. The diagonal is a bulk match. Slope is scale, intercept is location, a bow is shape, peeled tails are tails — or QC.
aliases: how to read a QQ plot
story: A Q–Q plot is a scatter of sample quantiles against theoretical quantiles of a reference law you named (often N(0,1) or χ²_1). Sort y₍₁₎ ≤ ⋯ ≤ y₍ₙ₎. Choose plotting positions, commonly (i − 1/2)/n or (i − 3/8)/(n + 1/4), invert the reference CDF, and plot (F⁻¹(pᵢ), y₍ᵢ₎). Points on the line y = x (after location-scale matching) mean the bulk of the sample is behaving like that reference.

Read the geometry before you read the anecdote. A vertical shift is location: the sample is centred elsewhere than the reference. A slope other than 1 is scale: the sample is more or less spread than the reference (on a Normal plot, slope estimates σ if the intercept estimates μ). A smooth bow is skew. Both tails peeling off the diagonal in the same fan is heavier tails (or a mixture). The opposite S is lighter tails. A few off-diagonal points at the ends can be discoveries, contaminants, or a bad assay — the plot does not caption itself.

In a TB methods section the two honest Q–Q jobs are residual checks (log MIC, GLM Pearson residuals) and GWAS inflation (χ² or −log₁₀ p Q–Q, λ_GC as a median summary). The glossary card wiki-qq is the encyclopedia name. This plate is how you refuse “the points looked fairly straight” as a Methods sentence.
deepTitle: Plotting positions, what bows, and what you must not delete
deep: Location-scale families (Normal, t after studentising) are judged after you allow an intercept and slope. A straight line with slope 2 on a standard Normal Q–Q is a variance problem, not a failed mean. Shape families (γ, χ²) are judged on curvature that location-scale cannot absorb.

Tails are noisy: order statistics at p = 1/n have large sampling variance. Do not declare a science result from three points off the diagonal without a named alternative (outlier rule, mixture, unmodelled structure).

GWAS: a χ²_1 Q–Q with λ_GC = median(χ²)/0.456 ≫ 1 is bulk inflation — population structure, polygenicity, or a miscalibrated test — not two starred SNPs. Manhattan without Q–Q is incomplete; Q–Q without a scientific null is theatre (stats-gwas).

Residual Q–Q in OLS assumes the error law you claimed, usually Normal after the mean structure. Curvature can be missing nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, or a heavy-tailed error. Straightening the plot by deleting the peak residuals is not a diagnostic; it is a cover-up (stats-ols-diagnostics).
A probability plot that uses expected Normal scores (Blom, van der Waerden) is the same idea with a slightly different F⁻¹(pᵢ). The reading rules do not change.

formulas.label: A common plotting position
formulas.expression: pᵢ = (i − 1/2) / n,    xᵢ = F₀⁻¹(pᵢ),    plot (xᵢ, y₍ᵢ₎)
formulas.note: Other positions exist. Name which one software used if the n is tiny.

formulas.label: Genomic inflation (χ²_1 Q–Q summary)
formulas.note: 0.456 ≈ median of χ²_1. λ ≫ 1 is bulk miscalibration, not a medal.

visual.caption: How a Q–Q plot is built and then read: sort the sample, pick plotting positions, invert the named reference, plot against the diagonal. Geometry after that is location, scale, shape, or tail — not a vibe.

example.title: Three readings of a Normal Q–Q of log-MIC residuals
example.setup: n = 40 OLS residuals on log MIC, plotted against N(0,1) quantiles after dividing by residual s (so a well-specified Normal error should hug y = x).

steps.title: Straight line, slope ≈ 1.1, intercept ≈ 0
steps.body: Bulk matches Normal; slightly extra scale. Check whether residual s was computed with the same n you plotted, and whether one lab batch is noisier — not a reason to invent a new mean structure yet.

steps.title: Both tails peel up/down, bulk still linear
steps.body: Heavier tails than Normal (or a two-point mixture of labs). A t error, a sandwich SE, or a robust loss is on the table. Deleting the six tail residuals to “fix the Q–Q” is not a residual analysis.

steps.title: Smooth upward bow in the right half
steps.body: Positive skew remaining after the log. The log was not enough, or the mean model is missing a clade. A Normal Q–Q is a shape check, not a proof that μ̂ is unbiased.

example.takeaway: Diagonal = bulk match to the named law. Slope, intercept, bow, and peeled tails are four different sentences.

check.prompt: On a standard Normal Q–Q plot (reference N(0,1)), a straight line with slope about 2 and intercept 0 most likely means:
choices: The sample mean is 2 and the SD is 1
The sample matches Normal location-scale with SD about twice the reference (σ ≈ 2), not a failed mean
You should delete half the points to restore slope 1
check.answer: The sample matches Normal location-scale with SD about twice the reference (σ ≈ 2), not a failed mean
check.why: In a location-scale family the Q–Q line’s slope is scale and the intercept is location. Slope 2 is σ, not μ = 2.

whyWrong.The sample mean is 2 and the SD is 1: Intercept 0 argues location still matches the reference centre; slope is scale.
whyWrong.The data are χ²_2: χ² is skewed; that would bow, not sit on a straight steep line through the origin.
whyWrong.You should delete half the points to res: That would hide scale, not diagnose it.

check.prompt: n = 10, i = 8, plotting position pᵢ = (i − 1/2)/n. What is p₈?
check.why: (8 − 0.5)/10 = 7.5/10 = 0.75. Using i/n = 0.8 is a different plotting convention; this plate named (i − 1/2)/n.

whyWrong.0.85: That would be (i − 0.5)/(n−1) or similar, not this formula.
whyWrong.0.5: That is the middle position, i = 5.5, not i = 8.

check.prompt: On the flow map, the split after “plot vs diagonal” exists because:
check.figureHint: Two end nodes: bulk location/scale versus tails shape/QC.
choices: A Q–Q plot only ever diagnoses means
A linear bulk and a peeled tail are different readings — location/scale versus shape, outliers, or QC
Plotting positions replace the reference law
GWAS λ_GC is the intercept of every Q–Q
check.answer: A linear bulk and a peeled tail are different readings — location/scale versus shape, outliers, or QC
check.why: The construction ends at the scatter. Interpretation forks: line geometry in the bulk versus what the ends are doing.

whyWrong.A Q–Q plot only ever diagnoses means: Means are the intercept; scale and shape live here too.
whyWrong.Plotting positions replace the reference: pᵢ chooses where on F₀ you invert; F₀ is still named.
whyWrong.GWAS λ_GC is the intercept of every Q–Q: λ_GC is a median χ² summary on one specialised Q–Q, not a universal intercept.
